hook.text: Portugal versus Spain. Monday. If you only watch one match before the final — make it this one. Let me show you why.

s1.text: Monday, three PM Eastern, AT&T Stadium in Dallas. Eighty thousand people. Two neighbours who cannot stand losing to each other. One goes home.

s2.text: And this isn't just a Round of 16 tie. On paper, these are two of the three best teams left in the tournament — meeting nine days before the final.

h1.text: There's fresh blood in this rivalry too. Last year's Nations League final? These exact two teams. Spain lifted the trophy — on penalties. Portugal have not forgotten that night.

h2.text: So before a ball is kicked, this match already has a script: revenge, or repeat. Everything else — the records, the kids, the legends — sits on top of that.

sp1.text: Now, the case for Spain — and honestly, it's frightening. Against Austria in the Round of 32, they produced the most complete performance of the whole tournament.

sp2.text: Three-nil. Oyarzabal scored twice, Pedro Porro added the third, and Austria barely touched the ball in the second half.

sp3.text: And here's the stat nobody believes: that was Spain's first World Cup knockout win since they lifted the trophy in 2010. Sixteen years of knockout heartbreak — gone in ninety minutes.

sp4.text: This Spain side suffocates you. They pass you to sleep, press you awake, and their front line is led by a teenager who plays like he's been doing it for a decade.

pt1.text: But now the case for Portugal — because their Round of 32 told you everything about who they are. It was ugly. It was desperate. And they found a way.

pt2.text: Croatia led them with forty minutes to go. Ronaldo dragged them level from the penalty spot. And in the ninety-fourth minute, substitute Gonçalo Ramos rose to a Leão cross and headed Portugal into this tie.

pt3.text: And about Ronaldo. Forty-one years old. This tournament he became the first player in history to score at SIX different World Cups. Nobody else has ever scored at more than five.

pt4.text: The World Cup is the only trophy he has never touched. He knows this is the last dance. And a wounded legend with nothing to lose is the most dangerous thing in football.

d1.text: Which brings us to the duel inside the match. Lamine Yamal is eighteen. Cristiano Ronaldo is forty-one. When Ronaldo made his World Cup debut, Yamal hadn't been born.

d2.text: The heir against the king. One is chasing his first World Cup story. The other is chasing his last. Monday, only one of those stories continues.

b1.text: Now zoom out to the bracket, because the stakes get bigger. The winner of this match gets the USA-Belgium winner in the quarterfinal at SoFi — a genuinely winnable game.

b2.text: Then a semifinal on July fourteenth. Then the final — where Messi's Argentina could be waiting. Win Monday, and you are two games from playing for everything.

b3.text: That's why this is a final in disguise. Whoever survives Monday becomes the favourite from the top half of the bracket. The loser gets a long summer of what-ifs.

p1.text: So, my prediction. The form says Spain — they're the best team in this tournament right now, and it isn't particularly close. The football brain says Spain too.

p2.text: But derbies don't read form guides. And Ronaldo in a last dance, in a knockout, against the one neighbour he'd crawl over glass to beat? I've watched football too long to call that safe.

p3.text: My call: Spain win — but it goes deep, it gets nasty, and if it reaches penalties, all bets are off. Drop your score prediction in the comments and roast mine.

cta.text: The full breakdown of the winner's road drops right after the final whistle — so subscribe. Monday. Three PM Eastern. Do not miss this one.
